If lower cost carbonaceous resources become more widely available (e.g., biogas, municipal solid waste and biomass gasification, CO capture, low- 2 cost renewables) as projected by IATA, alternative pathways are anticipated to gain significant market share from 2035 to 2050 (c.f., Figure 22). A key enabler to meeting these projections will be electricity availability and pricing, where, depending on study, PtL is seen as comprising >40% of total SAF production by 2050. While an exact electricity price ‘target’ will be case dependent and vary on numerous factors (e.g., availability of incentives, fossil jet market price dynamics, pathway efficiency), many of the techno-economic analyses conducted to date find that net electricity pricing on the order of ~$0.01–$0.02/kWh at scale is generally necessary to begin to approach parity with current incumbent fossil jet (Grim et al. 2022). SkyNRG’s annual SAF Market Outlook evaluates technology maturation. The 2025 study states that HEFA-based production will reach its upper limits based on feedstock availability around 2030 and that 82% of announced capacity are HEFA plants. Announced SAF capacity through 2030 is 6 billion gallons; however, delays and project cancellation have been common due to economic conditions and policy uncertainty (SkyNRG 2025). Figure 23 shows SkyNRG SAF plant capacity projections through 2050. The methodology of capacity through 2035 included an assessment of 390 SAF plant announcements (as of April 2025), where plants were excluded if they were determined to have a low probability of achieving production.4 Capacity was adjusted where market intelligence did not match public information and if total biofuel capacity was reported—SAF yield based on licensed technology was used (SkyNRG 2025). The 2035 projection assumes increased coprocessing at petroleum refineries contributing 700 million gallons and conversion of renewable diesel capacity contributing an additional 1.3 billion gallons (SkyNRG 2025). The 2050 capacity projection was modeled based on feedstock and policy assumptions. Figure 24 shows the 2030 breakout of capacity projections by region (SkyNRG 2025).
